items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — and this is the cleanest missed layup in the week's sample, because the customer asked for the agenda directly. Her opening was 'it's been a long time since I hired a mover but what kind of information would you need from me in order to give me an estimate?' That is an explicit request for the roadmap, and the answer she got was a single question: 'Yeah. Let's see. Are you moving from a home, an apartment or a townhome?' Ten seconds of 'Great question — I'll grab a few details about the home and the date, then I'll walk you through exactly how our pricing works and give you a real number. Takes about ten minutes. Sound good?' would have scored the section and set her expectations for a call she told him she was out of practice for.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up on an inbound call from a first-time customer who opened by introducing herself by name.

Additional rooms never asked. No garage, no attic, no patio, no storage unit probe on a 2500 sqft two-story townhome. She volunteered 'I'm not moving the outdoor furniture' and 'no refrigerators, they're staying with the house' on her own initiative.
Packing needs never asked, on a move she sized at fifty to sixty boxes.

Access concerns never asked — none, at either address. No parking, no truck access, no driveway, no HOA or gate, no loading restrictions. The origin is a duplex on Miller Avenue in 75206, dense Knox-Henderson street parking, and the destination is a Colleyville house, and neither was examined. On a job being priced at two 26-foot box trucks, whether both trucks can physically stage at the origin is a first-order question.
Walk distance never asked at either address, and no equivalents used.

Moving stressors never asked. She volunteered the real one herself — 'we're scheduled to close on Tuesday... nothing should go wrong but you never ever, ever know' — and he handled it well when it surfaced, but he never went looking for it.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener. He went straight from her date choice to 'So, we charge $101 per hour per mover.'

What's included was asserted but never listed. 'everything's everything needed to complete your move is included in that hourly rate' and 'that's quite literally all you're paying for' — with no gas, no truck, no taxes, no insurance, no pads, no wrap, no bands, no tools ever named. The entire value story of the hourly rate went unsaid, which matters because at $404 an hour she has nothing to weigh that number against.
Disassembly and reassembly never mentioned — not as an inclusion, not as a fee denial, and not as a time factor, on a move with dressers, a bed and a buffet going between two two-story homes.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. This is the most pointed miss on the call. She told him what she is worried about, unprompted: 'And she know fragile. No, I'm concerning the mirror. There's one buffet but it's like a sideboard. But you guys can lift that. But that's kind of heavy.' A customer naming a mirror and a heavy sideboard as her concerns is a customer asking to hear about damage coverage, and she never heard a word of it.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.
Clock start trigger never explained. She was never told the clock starts on site when the contract opens.
2.5 hour minimum never stated.

Fifteen-minute proration never stated. She is now booked, at $404 an hour, without knowing there is a minimum or how partial hours bill — which is the exact mechanic that makes 'you only pay for the time actually worked' mean something.

She asked for a smaller-home estimate and never got one. 'basically I think you'd be looking at an 1800 square foot house versus 25. If you know what I mean, since I don't have the bedroom dining room working for office, yeah, so give, give me an idea when an 1800 square foot would be.' That is a direct, specific pricing question. The answer was a truck-capacity explanation — 'we move with one size truck that's a 26 foot box truck that can typically fit around a fully furnished 1700 square foot home' — and the 1800 sqft number was never produced. She raised the same point a second time and it was redirected again.
Stairs never factored into the estimate. Both homes are two stories, the destination has a bedroom upstairs, and stairs were never named as a time driver anywhere in the quote.
Drive time never mentioned. Dallas 75206 to Colleyville 76034 is roughly thirty miles of billable clock on an eight-hour estimate, and it was never raised.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10, on a customer who is already doing the work. She is consigning a sectional and a rug, Goodwilling the contents of three rooms, selling office furniture and a chaise, and has a month to do it. She is performing a Save-Your-Ass purge on her own initiative, and nobody connected it to a shorter move and a smaller bill, or extended it to the loose small items that actually eat the clock.

No 'reply with any corrections' on the confirmation email — and this call badly needed it. The email address was captured phonetically through a genuinely difficult spelling exchange ('it's a different last name so it's more difficult Isabel.stoves S-P-O-L T-Z-M-A-N' → 'You were saying T. as in tango, correct?' → 'Yes, ST. Tango OL like liver, T-Z. Like Tom. Zebra and then man'), along with two addresses and two zip codes. Asking her to read it back and reply with corrections is the single highest-value fifteen seconds available on this call, and if that email address is wrong she never receives the confirmation at all and nobody finds out until October 12.
BOLDED key details at the top of the email never mentioned.
Hours and how to reach us never given. 'please do not hesitate to reach out' with no number and no hours, on a booking a month out.
Customer's name used twice — 'if you had to estimate the number of boxes Isabel' and 'Isabel, is this the best number to reach you at' — short of the 3+ standard.
top_strength: Zachary did something on this call that nobody else in the sample did, and it is directly relevant to the estimate-accuracy rock: he went and looked at the house. 'while I'm punching everything in, I can tend to be a little bit nosy. I looked up your current home that it says pending. Is this furniture accurate in the Zillow posting a little wooden secretary in the office with a Hutch behind it. Light brown leather chair in the same room?' That is verified inventory instead of self-reported inventory, obtained during dead air he would otherwise have spent typing. The customer's reaction tells you everything about how it landed: 'that's a great thing that you looked it up' and later 'I'm glad you did that, that's, that was very smart.' It also unlocked the most productive stretch of the call — she walked him through the listing photos room by room, flagging what goes and what stays ('the kitchen that you see all the stuff you see in the main room that will go with the exception of I'm not moving the TV and there's a chaise lounge in the living room that's gonna go with somebody else,' 'when you go upstairs one of the first pictures... that's not going with you, that's gonna be consigned'). He was disciplined about not over-recording it too, correctly deferring to the walkthrough: 'I won't add all these items cause obviously you know, if we wanted to do that virtual at a later date.' This is a technique worth putting in front of Tetet for the training deck. Beyond that, his truck-capacity explanation is the clearest in the batch and it did real work on a skeptical customer: 'we move with one size truck that's a 26 foot box truck that can typically fit around a fully furnished 1700 square foot home. Which is why, anything above that is why we by standard we send out a four man crew with two trucks just in the off chance that not everything fits into one.' When she asked the obvious follow-up — 'what if you came with two trucks and you only need one' — he answered it correctly and without hedging: 'you're paying more for the crew size basically cause it's just that $101 per hour, per mover.' Her reply was 'Okay, that makes sense.' He also read her anxiety correctly and answered it before she asked. She was superstitious about her Tuesday closing — 'nothing should go wrong but you never ever, ever know... I'll just take myself off your schedule' — and he volunteered the reversal risk-free: 'if you need to, to cancel or reschedule, there's no penalty or fee to do so... you can simply just reschedule to a new date with a click of a mouse.' Paired with the no-deposit line delivered earlier ('we don't require deposit or credit card to get this scheduled. But, we are first come, first serve... it's harder to add resources after the fact'), that is a well-judged commitment-risk close, and she booked.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: she asked a direct pricing question twice and never got an answer. 'give me an idea when an 1800 square foot would be' is about as explicit as a customer gets, and both times it was redirected into truck-capacity mechanics. She had just told him she is selling the office furniture, consigning an entire second living area and a sectional, Goodwilling three rooms' worth, has an empty third bedroom and no outdoor furniture — and his own stated logic is that a 26-foot truck holds a fully furnished 1700 sqft home, which means her post-purge load plausibly fits in one truck with a smaller crew. The answer she deserved was: 'Good question — if it really lands closer to 1800, that's typically a three-man crew on one truck, around six hours, so roughly $1,818. Let's book the four-man to be safe on the truck space, and then let's do that walkthrough once the consignment is out and I'll pull the resources back down if it fits.' That answers her question, keeps the booking, and sets up the walkthrough with a concrete reason. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: the quote on the books is four movers, two trucks, eight hours, $3,232, built on a 2500 sqft figure the customer explicitly and repeatedly told him overstates the load. This is the same pattern as the Dueck call this week — a form-field square footage beating live customer testimony — and it is the conservative-padding-on-large-homes half of the failure mode exactly. Zachary's justification is more defensible than most (truck capacity is genuinely a step function, and it is harder to add resources than remove them, which he explained well), but the customer never received a number for the load she actually described, and the difference between a four-man and a three-man crew over six to eight hours is $600 to $800 of her money. Two concrete asks: put the walkthrough on the calendar now rather than leaving it as 'maybe, I'll go ahead and take you up on that virtual walkthrough before the twelfth' — she is willing and the consignment timing is known — and note in the file that the quote is pending a downward revision, so it does not sit unchallenged for four weeks. Second priority: pricing scored 8/20 and clock scored 1/4, which is the weakest combined showing in the week's sample from a rep who otherwise ran a good call. He asserted 'everything needed to complete your move is included in that hourly rate' without ever listing a single thing, never said 'no deposit' until the anxiety surfaced on its own, and never mentioned the 2.5 hour minimum, the clock start trigger, or the fifteen-minute proration at all. She is booked at $404 an hour and does not know how the clock works. Third, the differentiators. She told him exactly where she is worried — 'I'm concerning the mirror. There's one buffet but it's like a sideboard... that's kind of heavy' — and No Worries Damage Coverage was the answer to that sentence and never came. Add the twenty-second block: '$2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse, which matters for that mirror and the buffet; you'll get an email with a photo of your actual mover a few days out; and if we miss your arrival window we start discounting immediately.' Fourth, verify that email address. It was captured through a hard phonetic exchange with at least one apparent mismatch in the transcript, and a confirmation email that bounces on a booking four weeks out is a move nobody finds out about until move week.
phone_presence_notes: Real personality and collaborative energy once he warmed up — the self-deprecating framing on the Zillow lookup ('I can tend to be a little bit nosy') turned a data-entry pause into the most engaged stretch of the call, and he matched her superstition about the closing with genuine lightness ('if for whatever reason it doesn't, my fingers crossed, everything goes well') — but the first half is transactional to the point of abruptness: no warm-up, no 'how are you,' and a direct question from the customer about how the process works answered with a one-line qualifier.
